overview: A shell script is a plain text file containing a list of commands you would otherwise type one at a time into the terminal; the shell reads the file top to bottom and runs each line, letting you automate a whole sequence of steps with a single command.

The first line is usually a shebang like #!/bin/bash that tells the operating system which interpreter should run the file; after you make the file executable with 'chmod +x', you can run it as './script.sh' just like any other program.

The core building blocks are variables (name=value), running one command's output into another with command substitution $(...), reading arguments the caller passed ($1, $2, $@), checking whether the last command succeeded via its exit code ($?), and control flow (if/then, for, while, case) that lets a script make decisions and repeat work.
learningObjectives: Write a runnable bash script from scratch: add a shebang, make it executable with chmod +x, and run it, understanding the difference between './script.sh' and 'bash script.sh'.

Use variables, quoting ("$var"), command substitution $(...), positional arguments ($1, $@, $#), and exit codes ($?) correctly, avoiding the classic beginner traps around spaces and unquoted variables.

Control a script's flow with if/elif/else, for and while loops, and case, and write safe, production-ready scripts using 'set -euo pipefail', redirection (> >> 2>&1), functions, and 'trap' for cleanup.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A shell script is an executable text file interpreted line by line by a Unix shell (commonly bash, the Bourne-Again Shell), where each line is either a command, a variable assignment, or a control-flow construct. The shebang (#!) on the first line names the interpreter the kernel should invoke to run the file. The shell resolves variables (introduced by name=value with no surrounding spaces and referenced as $name or "$name"), performs command substitution ($(command) replaces itself with that command's standard output), and passes positional parameters ($1..$9, $@ for all, $# for the count) to the running script. Every command returns an integer exit status (0 for success, non-zero for failure), available in the special variable $? and used by control-flow constructs such as if, while, and until, and by the test operators [ ] and [[ ]]. Streams can be redirected: > overwrites a file, >> appends, and 2>&1 merges standard error into standard output. Options like 'set -e' (exit on error), 'set -u' (error on unset variables), and 'set -o pipefail' (a pipeline fails if any stage fails) make scripts fail fast, and 'trap' registers commands to run when the script exits or receives a signal.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine you make coffee the same way every morning: fill the kettle, boil it, grind beans, pour, wait four minutes. A shell script is like writing that recipe down once so a helper can follow it exactly, every day, without you standing over them. Each line of the script is one instruction. The shebang at the top is a note that says 'follow this recipe using the bash cook, not some other cook'. 'chmod +x' is putting the recipe on the fridge where it is allowed to be used. A variable is a labeled jar - you write name="Sunday batch" and later the script reads that label instead of you repeating it. Reading $1 is the script looking at what you handed it when you asked it to start ('make me the July 1st batch'). The exit code is the helper telling you afterwards 'done, no problems' (0) or 'something went wrong' (a non-zero number) so an automatic scheduler knows whether to raise an alarm. if/for/while are the recipe saying 'if the beans jar is empty, stop and tell me', 'for each of these seven days, run the load', and 'while the download hasn't finished, keep waiting'.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Shell scripting goes back to the original Unix shell written by Ken Thompson in the early 1970s at Bell Labs, but the language most scripts are written in today descends from the Bourne shell (sh), created by Stephen Bourne in 1979, which introduced variables, control flow, and the scripting features still used now. In 1989 the GNU project released bash (Bourne-Again Shell) as a free, backward-compatible superset with many conveniences, and it became the default shell on most Linux distributions and, for years, on macOS. Competing shells like the C shell (csh), KornShell (ksh), and later zsh added their own features, but bash and POSIX sh remain the lingua franca for portable scripts. The shebang mechanism (#!) was added to Unix in the early 1980s so the kernel could pick the right interpreter automatically. For data engineers, shell scripts have been the durable 'glue' of pipelines for decades - wrapping programs, moving files, and wiring jobs into schedulers like cron - and even as orchestration tools such as Airflow rose, the underlying tasks they run are very often still shell scripts.

whyItMatters.business: Shell scripts turn a manual, error-prone checklist into a repeatable, one-command process, so routine data loads and reports run the same way every time regardless of who is on shift, reducing costly human mistakes and freeing engineers for higher-value work.
whyItMatters.engineering: Almost every data pipeline has 'glue' steps - download a file, check it exists, run a Python job, move the result, notify on failure - and shell is the fastest, most universal way to wire those steps together and return a clear success/failure code that a scheduler can act on.
whyItMatters.scalability: A single well-written script can loop over hundreds of dated input files or run across many servers unchanged, so the same few lines that handle one day's load scale to a full backfill or a fleet without rewriting the logic.
whyItMatters.cost: Scripts run on the servers you already have with tools that ship for free on every Linux box, so automating glue work needs no new licenses or infrastructure, and failing fast (set -e) avoids wasted compute on jobs that were doomed after the first error.
whyItMatters.reliability: By checking exit codes, using 'set -euo pipefail', and exiting non-zero on failure, a script makes problems visible to the scheduler instead of silently continuing on bad data, and 'trap' guarantees cleanup (removing temp files, releasing locks) even when a job aborts.

coreComponents.name: Shebang, permissions, and execution
coreComponents.definition: The shebang (#!/bin/bash or #!/usr/bin/env bash) on line one names the interpreter; 'chmod +x' marks the file executable; you then run it as './script.sh' or explicitly with 'bash script.sh'.
coreComponents.purpose: To make a text file behave like a real program the operating system can launch, using the correct interpreter, without the caller having to know it is a bash script.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Declare the interpreter so the kernel runs the file with bash; grant execute permission so './script.sh' is allowed; distinguish running via the shebang (./script.sh) from bypassing it by naming the interpreter (bash script.sh).

coreComponents.name: Variables, quoting, and command substitution
coreComponents.definition: Variables are set as name=value (no spaces around =) and read as $name or "$name"; command substitution $(command) captures a command's output into a value.
coreComponents.purpose: To store and reuse values (paths, dates, filenames), build commands dynamically, and avoid repeating literals so a script is readable and easy to change.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Assign values without spaces around =, always quote expansions ("$var") to survive spaces and empties, capture output with $(date +%F) or $(wc -l < file), and keep names descriptive.

coreComponents.name: Arguments and exit codes
coreComponents.definition: Positional parameters $1, $2, ... hold the arguments passed to the script; $@ is all of them, $# is how many; every command sets an exit status readable as $? (0 = success, non-zero = failure).
coreComponents.purpose: To let one script be reused with different inputs (a date, a filename) and to detect and propagate success or failure so schedulers and later steps can react.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Read inputs from $1/$2/$@, validate their count with $#, check the previous command's result with $?, and exit with a chosen code ('exit 0' success, 'exit 1' failure) so callers know what happened.
coreComponents.examples: date="$1" | echo "got $# args" | for f in "$@"; do ...; done | if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then exit 1; fi

coreComponents.name: Control flow and safety options
coreComponents.definition: if/elif/else/fi with test operators [ ] and [[ ]], for and while loops, and case for branching; 'set -euo pipefail' and 'trap' make scripts fail fast and clean up.
coreComponents.purpose: To let a script make decisions (does the input file exist?), repeat work (loop over each day), and behave safely by stopping on the first error and cleaning up afterwards.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Branch on conditions with if/case, iterate with for/while, test files and values with [ -f file ] or [[ $x -gt 0 ]], enable strict mode with 'set -euo pipefail', and register cleanup with 'trap cleanup EXIT'.
coreComponents.examples: if [ -f "$file" ]; then ...; fi | for d in $(seq 1 7); do ...; done | while read line; do ...; done | set -euo pipefail | trap cleanup EXIT

internalWorking: When you run './script.sh', the kernel opens the file, reads the shebang on the first line (for example #!/bin/bash), and launches that interpreter with the script file as its input; if there were no shebang and no execute permission, the OS would refuse to run it, which is why 'chmod +x' matters. Running 'bash script.sh' instead ignores the shebang entirely and hands the file to the bash you named.

The interpreter reads the file one logical line at a time, expanding it before execution: it splits the line into words, substitutes variables ($var becomes its value), runs any command substitutions ($(...)), performs quoting and globbing (* expands to matching filenames), and only then executes the resulting command - which is exactly why unquoted variables containing spaces get split into multiple words and can break a script.

Each command runs as a process and returns an integer exit status to the shell, stored in $?. Zero means success and any non-zero value means some kind of failure. Control-flow constructs are built on this: 'if cmd; then' runs the then-branch when cmd's exit status is 0, and '&&' / '||' chain commands based on success or failure of the previous one.

'set -e' tells the shell to stop the whole script the moment any command exits non-zero (instead of blindly continuing), 'set -u' makes it error out if you reference a variable that was never set (catching typos), and 'set -o pipefail' makes a pipeline like 'a | b' report failure if any stage fails, not just the last one. Together, 'set -euo pipefail' turns silent partial failures into loud, immediate stops.

'trap COMMAND EXIT' registers a command to run automatically whenever the script exits for any reason - normal completion, an error under set -e, or a signal like Ctrl+C (SIGINT) - which is how scripts guarantee they remove temporary files, release locks, or send a final notification even when they abort. The script's own final exit code (from 'exit N' or the last command) is what a scheduler like cron reads to decide whether the job succeeded.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Shebang tells kernel which interpreter -> chmod +x makes file runnable -> ./script.sh launches bash on the file -> shell reads each line, expands variables and $(...) -> commands run as processes, each returning an exit code in $? -> if/for/while branch and loop on those codes -> set -euo pipefail stops on first failure -> trap runs cleanup on exit -> script exits 0 (success) or non-zero (failure) which the scheduler reads
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A scheduler (cron) runs './run_etl.sh 2026-07-01' at 2am. The kernel reads the shebang '#!/usr/bin/env bash' and launches bash on the file; bash reads 'set -euo pipefail' so the script will stop on the first error, treat unset variables as errors, and fail if any piped stage fails.

2. The script captures inputs and derived values: 'run_date="$1"' reads the argument passed by cron, and 'log_file="/var/log/etl/etl_${run_date}.log"' builds a dated log path using variable expansion; it registers 'trap cleanup EXIT' so temporary files are removed no matter how the run ends.

3. It validates preconditions with control flow: 'if [ ! -f "$input" ]; then echo "missing input" >&2; exit 1; fi'. Because set -e is on, if the input file is missing the script exits with code 1 immediately, and cron sees a failed job.

4. The input exists, so the script runs the real work - 'python3 transform.py --date "$run_date" >> "$log_file" 2>&1' - redirecting both normal output and errors into the dated log. The shell stores that command's exit status in $?; under set -e a non-zero status would abort the script here.

5. On success the script logs a timestamped 'DONE' line and 'exit 0'; on any failure the trap fires to clean up temp files and the script exits non-zero, so the scheduler records the failure, alerts the on-call engineer, and the bad run does not silently pass downstream.

keyTerminology.meaning: The first line of a script, like #!/bin/bash or #!/usr/bin/env bash, that tells the operating system which interpreter to use to run the file.
keyTerminology.importance: Without it (and without naming the interpreter explicitly), the OS may run your script with the wrong shell or refuse to run it, causing confusing errors.

keyTerminology.meaning: The integer a command returns when it finishes: 0 means success, any non-zero value means failure; the last command's code is stored in the special variable $?.
keyTerminology.importance: Schedulers, control flow, and later steps all decide what to do based on exit codes, so returning the right code is how a script signals success or failure.

keyTerminology.meaning: The arguments passed to a script: $1 is the first, $2 the second, $@ expands to all of them, and $# is how many were given.
keyTerminology.importance: They let a single script be reused with different inputs (a date, a filename) instead of hard-coding values, which is the basis of parameterized pipeline steps.

keyTerminology.meaning: Syntax that runs a command and replaces itself with that command's standard output, for example today=$(date +%F) stores today's date in a variable.
keyTerminology.importance: It lets scripts compute values dynamically - dates, counts, file lists - and feed them into other commands, which is essential for real ETL glue logic.

keyTerminology.meaning: Three options combined: -e exits on any command error, -u errors on unset variables, and -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails.
keyTerminology.importance: It turns silent partial failures into immediate, visible stops, which prevents a broken script from continuing on bad data and corrupting downstream results.

importantConcepts.concept: No spaces around = in assignments (and always quote when you read)
importantConcepts.explanation: In the shell, 'name=value' assigns a variable, but the shell is picky: there must be NO spaces around the equals sign. Writing 'name = value' is not an assignment at all - the shell reads it as running a command called 'name' with the arguments '=' and 'value', which fails confusingly. So it is 'DATA_DIR=/data/raw', never 'DATA_DIR = /data/raw'. When you later use the variable, wrap it in double quotes: "$DATA_DIR". Quoting matters because if a value contains spaces (like a path '/data/July batch') or is empty, an unquoted $DATA_DIR gets split into multiple words or disappears, breaking commands like 'rm $file' in dangerous ways. The reliable habit is: assign with no spaces, read with double quotes.

importantConcepts.concept: Exit codes drive everything - make failures loud
importantConcepts.explanation: Every command returns an exit code, and the shell's whole control model is built on it: 0 is success, non-zero is failure. 'if grep -q ERROR log; then ...' runs the branch when grep's exit code is 0 (it found a match). The last command's code lives in $?. This matters enormously for pipelines because a scheduler like cron or Airflow decides whether a job passed or failed purely from the script's final exit code. If your script hits an error but still ends with exit 0 (or just runs off the end after a failing command), the scheduler thinks everything is fine and the bad data flows downstream. The fixes are to enable 'set -e' so errors abort the script, to check '$?' or use 'if ! command; then' where you need custom handling, and to call 'exit 1' explicitly when you detect a problem so failure is unmistakable.

importantConcepts.concept: set -euo pipefail: safe scripts fail fast
importantConcepts.explanation: By default the shell is forgiving in exactly the wrong way: if a command fails, it just prints the error and keeps going to the next line, and referencing a misspelled variable silently gives an empty string. 'set -e' fixes the first: any command that fails aborts the script immediately. 'set -u' fixes the second: using an unset variable becomes an error, so a typo like $INPTU (instead of $INPUT) is caught instead of quietly expanding to nothing. 'set -o pipefail' handles pipelines: normally 'download | gunzip | load' reports only the exit code of the last stage, so if 'download' fails but 'load' succeeds on empty input, the pipeline looks successful; pipefail makes the whole pipeline fail if any stage does. The idiom 'set -euo pipefail' near the top of every serious script converts these silent, dangerous behaviors into loud, immediate failures - the single most important habit for reliable glue scripts.

importantConcepts.concept: trap for cleanup and running ./script.sh vs bash script.sh
importantConcepts.explanation: Two operational details trip up beginners. First, 'trap' lets you register a command to run whenever the script exits, no matter how: 'trap cleanup EXIT' guarantees your cleanup function runs on normal completion, on an error under set -e, or when the user hits Ctrl+C - which is how you reliably delete temp files or release a lock file even when a job aborts halfway. Second, there are two ways to run a script and they behave differently: './script.sh' asks the OS to execute the file, which requires execute permission ('chmod +x') and uses the interpreter named in the shebang; 'bash script.sh' instead starts a new bash and tells it to read the file, which ignores the shebang and does not need execute permission. 'bash script.sh' is handy for a quick test or when a file is not executable, but the standard, self-documenting way to ship a script is with a shebang plus chmod +x so it runs as './script.sh'.

variationsAndTypes: **Interpreters (the shebang target):** #!/bin/bash (bash-specific features), #!/bin/sh (portable POSIX shell, fewer features), and #!/usr/bin/env bash (finds bash on PATH, more portable across systems where bash lives in different locations).

**Test constructs:** the classic '[ ... ]' (the 'test' command, POSIX, needs careful quoting), the bash-enhanced '[[ ... ]]' (safer with unquoted variables, supports && and pattern matching), and '(( ... ))' for pure arithmetic comparisons.

**Loops:** 'for x in list; do ... done' (iterate over items or files), 'for ((i=0;i<n;i++))' (C-style counting), 'while condition; do ... done' (repeat until a condition changes), and 'until condition' (loop until it becomes true) - commonly paired with 'read' to process files line by line.

**Redirection and pipes:** '>' overwrite a file, '>>' append, '2>' redirect only errors, '2>&1' merge errors into standard output, '<' read from a file, and '|' pipe one command's output into another to build data-processing chains.

**Ways to structure and secure scripts:** plain top-to-bottom scripts, function-based scripts (reusable blocks called like commands), scripts wrapped by a scheduler (cron/Airflow) versus run interactively, and hardened scripts using 'set -euo pipefail' plus 'trap' for cleanup.
advantages: **Universal and free:** bash ships on virtually every Linux/Unix server, so scripts run anywhere with no installation, licenses, or extra dependencies.
**Perfect glue:** shell excels at wiring existing programs together - run a Python job, move files, call an API tool - which is exactly what most pipeline steps need.
**Fast to write and iterate:** a few lines automate a manual checklist immediately, with no build step, so you go from idea to working automation in minutes.
**Clear success/failure signaling:** exit codes let schedulers and later steps react automatically, so failures are detected instead of silently ignored.
**Composable and readable:** pipes, redirection, variables, and functions let you build up complex behavior from small, understandable pieces.
disadvantages: **Error-prone syntax:** the picky rules around spaces, quoting, and [ ] versus [[ ]] make it easy to write bugs that fail silently or behave differently on other systems.
**Poor for complex logic and data:** anything involving rich data structures, math, or intricate parsing is far cleaner in Python; large shell scripts become hard to read and maintain.
**Portability pitfalls:** a script that works in bash may break in sh or on macOS's older bash, and small differences in tool versions (GNU vs BSD) cause surprises.
**Weak testing and debugging:** shell has limited built-in testing support, and debugging relies on 'set -x' tracing and print statements rather than a real debugger.
**Easy to do something destructive:** an unquoted variable or a bad glob in an 'rm' command can delete the wrong files, and there is no undo - small mistakes have big consequences.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use shell scripts for glue and orchestration of the small: launching programs, checking that files exist, moving and renaming data between stages, looping over dated inputs, logging with timestamps, and returning a clean exit code to a scheduler. They are ideal when the logic is a sequence of command invocations rather than heavy data manipulation.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid shell for anything with complex data structures, non-trivial math, intricate string parsing, or logic that spans hundreds of lines - reach for Python instead. Also avoid piling business logic into a script when a real orchestrator (Airflow) or a proper program would be clearer, testable, and more maintainable. When correctness and readability matter more than a five-minute setup, prefer a language built for it.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A shell script is like a written recipe card taped inside a kitchen. The shebang is the note at the top - 'prepare using the bread oven, not the pizza oven' - telling everyone which appliance (interpreter) to use. 'chmod +x' is the manager approving the card so cooks are allowed to follow it. Variables are the labeled prep containers ('today's dough', 'the 2pm batch') the recipe refers to instead of describing the contents each time. The arguments you pass are the order slip handed in with the card ('make the July 1st batch'). Each step returns a thumbs-up or thumbs-down: an exit code. 'set -euo pipefail' is a strict head chef standing over the line who stops everything the instant a step goes wrong instead of letting a mistake continue down the counter. A loop is 'repeat this plating for each of the seven plates'. And 'trap' is the standing rule 'no matter what happens - even if you have to abandon the dish - wipe down your station before you leave', guaranteeing cleanup even when things go sideways.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Spaces around the = in a variable assignment are fine, just like in most programming languages.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In the shell they are not. 'name=value' assigns; 'name = value' is interpreted as running a command 'name' with arguments '=' and 'value', which fails. The equals sign must have no spaces on either side - this is one of the most common beginner errors.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Quoting variables is optional and just clutters the script.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Quoting is essential. An unquoted $file that contains spaces gets split into multiple words, and an empty variable can vanish entirely, so 'rm $file' can behave very differently from 'rm "$file"'. Always use double quotes around expansions unless you have a specific reason not to.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A script automatically stops if one of its commands fails.
commonMisconceptions.reality: By default it does not - the shell prints the error and keeps running the next line, which can compound a failure or run steps on bad data. You have to opt in with 'set -e' (and ideally 'set -euo pipefail') to make the script abort on the first error.

productionConsiderations.scalability: A single parameterized script scales by being invoked many times with different arguments (per date, per file, per host) rather than being rewritten; drive it from a scheduler that fans out runs, keep the script itself small and idempotent, and pass inputs as arguments so the same code handles one day or a full backfill.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Start every serious script with 'set -euo pipefail' so it fails fast, validate inputs (file exists, arguments present) before doing work, exit non-zero on any failure so the scheduler notices, and use 'trap ... EXIT' to guarantee cleanup and a final status log even when the run aborts.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Make scripts idempotent (safe to re-run) by writing to temp files and moving them into place only on success, and by checkpointing progress; wrap flaky steps like downloads in a retry loop with backoff so a transient error does not fail the whole job.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Log every run with timestamps to a dated file (redirect stdout and stderr with '>> file 2>&1'), record start, key steps, and the final exit status, and expose success/failure through the exit code so the scheduler and any alerting can see it without parsing logs.
productionConsiderations.security: Never hard-code secrets in scripts - read them from environment variables or a secrets manager; quote all variables to avoid injection and accidental globbing, avoid running scripts as root unless required, and be extremely careful with 'rm' and variables that could be empty or contain unexpected characters.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Failing fast with set -e avoids spending compute on a job that was already doomed; skip work that is already done (idempotency checks), and prefer lightweight shell glue over spinning up heavy runtimes for simple file moves and checks.
productionConsiderations.performance: Shell startup is cheap, but calling external commands in a tight loop is not - minimize per-iteration process launches, use built-ins and single passes (e.g. one 'find' or 'xargs') where possible, and avoid re-reading large files repeatedly; for heavy data crunching, hand off to a purpose-built tool rather than looping in bash.

codeExamples.title: A well-structured ETL wrapper script (shebang, strict mode, variables, arguments, input check, logging, exit codes)
codeExamples.overview: A parameterized wrapper that a scheduler runs with a date; it validates its input, runs a Python ETL step, logs with timestamps, and exits non-zero on failure so the scheduler detects it.
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run_etl.sh - wrap a daily ETL step with logging and clear exit codes
# Usage: ./run_etl.sh YYYY-MM-DD

set -euo pipefail   # -e stop on error, -u error on unset vars, pipefail catch pipe failures

# --- 1) Read and validate the argument the caller passed ---
if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 YYYY-MM-DD" >&2   # >&2 sends the message to standard error
  exit 2
fi
run_date="$1"

# --- 2) Set up paths using variables and command substitution ---
DATA_DIR="/data/raw"
input_file="${DATA_DIR}/events_${run_date}.csv"
log_file="/var/log/etl/etl_${run_date}.log"
started_at="$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')"

# A tiny helper so every log line is timestamped
log() { echo "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S') $*" | tee -a "$log_file"; }

log "START etl for ${run_date} (began ${started_at})"

# --- 3) Check the input file exists before doing any work ---
if [ ! -f "$input_file" ]; then
  log "ERROR missing input file: ${input_file}"
  exit 1   # non-zero tells the scheduler this run FAILED
fi

# --- 4) Run the real work; both stdout and stderr go to the log ---
log "Running transform on ${input_file}"
python3 /opt/etl/transform.py --date "$run_date" --input "$input_file" >> "$log_file" 2>&1

# --- 5) If we got here, set -e means every command above succeeded ---
row_count="$(wc -l < "$input_file")"
log "DONE etl for ${run_date}: processed ${row_count} input rows"
exit 0
codeExamples.breakdown: The shebang '#!/usr/bin/env bash' finds bash via PATH. 'set -euo pipefail' makes the script fail fast on errors, unset variables, and broken pipes. '$#' is the argument count, so 'if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]' rejects the wrong number of arguments and 'exit 2' signals a usage error; '$0' is the script's own name. Variables are assigned with no spaces around = and read quoted ("$run_date"). Command substitution '$(date ...)' builds a timestamp and '$(wc -l < "$input_file")' counts rows. The 'log()' function timestamps and tees each message to the log. '[ ! -f "$input_file" ]' tests that the file is missing and 'exit 1' reports failure. The python step redirects both streams with '>> "$log_file" 2>&1'. Reaching the end means success, so it logs DONE and 'exit 0'.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
2026-07-02 02:00:01 START etl for 2026-07-01 (began 2026-07-02 02:00:01)
2026-07-02 02:00:01 Running transform on /data/raw/events_2026-07-01.csv
2026-07-02 02:00:47 DONE etl for 2026-07-01: processed 184203 input rows

# If the input file were missing instead:
2026-07-02 02:00:01 START etl for 2026-07-01 (began 2026-07-02 02:00:01)
2026-07-02 02:00:01 ERROR missing input file: /data/raw/events_2026-07-01.csv
# (script exits with code 1; run: echo $?  ->  1)
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting 'chmod +x run_etl.sh' means './run_etl.sh' fails with 'Permission denied' - either chmod it or run 'bash run_etl.sh'. Writing 'run_date = "$1"' with spaces breaks the assignment. Omitting quotes around "$input_file" breaks on paths with spaces. Without 'set -e', a failing python step would not stop the script, and it would wrongly log DONE and exit 0.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add 'trap' to clean up temp files on exit (see the next example). Validate the date format with a regex or 'date -d "$run_date"' before using it. Use 'exec >> "$log_file" 2>&1' near the top to redirect all output to the log in one place. Return distinct exit codes (1 = data problem, 2 = usage error) so the scheduler can react differently.

codeExamples.title: Loop over daily input files with a trap for cleanup and per-file error handling
codeExamples.overview: Process a range of dated files in a for loop, using a temporary directory that is always cleaned up via trap, counting successes and failures, and exiting non-zero if any day failed.
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# process_range.sh - load every daily file from START to END (inclusive)
# Usage: ./process_range.sh 2026-07-01 2026-07-03

set -euo pipefail

start_date="$1"
end_date="$2"
DATA_DIR="/data/raw"

# --- Create a temp workspace and guarantee it is removed on exit ---
tmp_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
cleanup() {
  echo "Cleaning up ${tmp_dir}"
  rm -rf "$tmp_dir"
}
trap cleanup EXIT   # runs on normal exit, on error (set -e), or Ctrl+C

failures=0
processed=0

# --- Walk each date from start to end using GNU date arithmetic ---
current="$start_date"
while [[ "$current" != "$end_date" ]] || { load_last=1; true; }; do
  input_file="${DATA_DIR}/events_${current}.csv"
  echo "--- ${current} ---"

  if [ ! -f "$input_file" ]; then
    echo "WARN missing ${input_file}, skipping" >&2
    failures=$((failures + 1))
  else
    # Run one day; if it fails, record it but keep going to the next day
    if python3 /opt/etl/load_day.py --date "$current" --input "$input_file"; then
      processed=$((processed + 1))
    else
      echo "ERROR load failed for ${current}" >&2
      failures=$((failures + 1))
    fi
  fi

  [[ -n "${load_last:-}" ]] && break
  current="$(date -d "$current + 1 day" '+%Y-%m-%d')"   # next day
done

echo "Summary: processed=${processed} failures=${failures}"
[ "$failures" -eq 0 ] || exit 1   # non-zero if any day failed
codeExamples.breakdown: 'mktemp -d' creates a unique temp directory; the 'cleanup' function 'rm -rf's it, and 'trap cleanup EXIT' guarantees that runs however the script ends. The 'while' loop walks each date, and 'date -d "$current + 1 day"' advances the date by one day. For each day, '[ ! -f "$input_file" ]' checks the file exists; missing files are warned about (to stderr with '>&2') and counted as failures. The inner 'if python3 ...; then' pattern runs the load and branches on its exit code without letting set -e abort the whole run, so one bad day does not stop the rest; counters use arithmetic '$((...))'. Finally it prints a summary and '[ "$failures" -eq 0 ] || exit 1' exits non-zero if anything failed.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
--- 2026-07-01 ---
Loaded 2026-07-01 (184203 rows)
--- 2026-07-02 ---
WARN missing /data/raw/events_2026-07-02.csv, skipping
--- 2026-07-03 ---
Loaded 2026-07-03 (176544 rows)
Summary: processed=2 failures=1
Cleaning up /tmp/tmp.a1B2c3D4e5
# script exits with code 1 because one day failed  ->  echo $?  gives  1
codeExamples.commonIssues: Under 'set -e', calling a failing command outside an 'if'/'||' guard aborts the whole loop - wrap fallible per-item work in 'if cmd; then ... else ... fi' so one failure does not kill the batch. Forgetting the trap leaves temp files behind on crashes. 'date -d' is GNU-specific; macOS/BSD 'date' uses different flags. Referencing 'load_last' with 'set -u' requires the '${load_last:-}' default to avoid an unset-variable error.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'seq' or a simpler explicit list of dates when the range is small and known. Process independent days in parallel with '&' plus 'wait', or with 'xargs -P', to speed up large backfills. Write each day's output to a temp file and move it into place only on success for idempotency. Emit the summary as a structured line so a scheduler can parse processed/failures counts.

codeExamples.title: A function-based script with a retry loop for a flaky download step
codeExamples.overview: A reusable, function-organized script that retries a flaky download with backoff, logs each attempt, and only proceeds to the next step once the download succeeds - exiting non-zero if all retries fail.
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# fetch_and_load.sh - download a file with retries, then load it
# Usage: ./fetch_and_load.sh https://example.com/data.csv /data/raw/data.csv

set -euo pipefail

URL="$1"
DEST="$2"
MAX_RETRIES=3
RETRY_DELAY=5   # seconds, doubles each attempt

log() { echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') $*"; }

# --- Reusable function: retry a flaky download with exponential backoff ---
download_with_retry() {
  local url="$1" dest="$2"
  local attempt=1 delay="$RETRY_DELAY"

  while [ "$attempt" -le "$MAX_RETRIES" ]; do
    log "Attempt ${attempt}/${MAX_RETRIES}: downloading ${url}"
    if curl -fsS --max-time 30 -o "$dest" "$url"; then
      log "Download OK -> ${dest}"
      return 0            # success: leave the function with code 0
    fi
    log "Attempt ${attempt} failed; retrying in ${delay}s"
    sleep "$delay"
    attempt=$((attempt + 1))
    delay=$((delay * 2))  # exponential backoff
  done

  log "ERROR download failed after ${MAX_RETRIES} attempts"
  return 1               # all retries exhausted
}

load_file() {
  local file="$1"
  log "Loading ${file}"
  python3 /opt/etl/load.py --input "$file"
}

# --- Main flow ---
log "Job start for ${URL}"
if ! download_with_retry "$URL" "$DEST"; then
  exit 1   # download never succeeded; fail the job
fi
load_file "$DEST"
log "Job complete"
exit 0
codeExamples.breakdown: Functions are defined as 'name() { ... }' and called like commands. 'local' keeps variables scoped inside the function. 'download_with_retry' loops up to MAX_RETRIES times; 'curl -fsS' fails on HTTP errors (-f), stays quiet but shows errors (-sS), and 'if curl ...; then return 0' exits the function successfully on the first good download. On failure it logs, 'sleep "$delay"' waits, then doubles the delay ('delay=$((delay * 2))') for exponential backoff. If the loop ends without success it 'return 1'. In the main flow, 'if ! download_with_retry ...; then exit 1' propagates a total failure as a non-zero script exit; only on success does it call 'load_file', which runs the Python loader. 'exit 0' marks overall success.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
14:22:03 Job start for https://example.com/data.csv
14:22:03 Attempt 1/3: downloading https://example.com/data.csv
14:22:04 Attempt 1 failed; retrying in 5s
14:22:09 Attempt 2/3: downloading https://example.com/data.csv
14:22:10 Attempt 2 failed; retrying in 10s
14:22:20 Attempt 3/3: downloading https://example.com/data.csv
14:22:22 Download OK -> /data/raw/data.csv
14:22:22 Loading /data/raw/data.csv
14:22:41 Job complete
# overall exit code: 0
codeExamples.commonIssues: Without 'curl -f', curl exits 0 even on a 404 and you 'succeed' in downloading an error page - always use -f so HTTP failures become non-zero exits. Forgetting 'return' values means the calling 'if' misjudges success. Under 'set -e', not guarding the download call with 'if !' would abort before your retry logic runs. Retrying without a max or a delay can hammer a struggling server (a retry storm).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add jitter (a small random extra delay) to backoff so many jobs do not retry in lockstep. Only retry on transient errors (timeouts, 5xx), not on permanent ones (404, auth failures). Verify the download (checksum or non-empty size) before treating it as success. Factor 'log', 'download_with_retry', and 'load_file' into a shared library file sourced with '. lib.sh' so multiple scripts reuse them.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An analytics team needs a nightly job that pulls the previous day's event export, loads it into the warehouse, and must be run automatically by cron. It has to detect a missing or empty file, retry a flaky download, log everything with timestamps for auditing, clean up temp files, and - crucially - exit non-zero on any failure so cron's alerting fires and the bad run never silently passes downstream.
endToEndExample.inputData: A daily CSV export named events_YYYY-MM-DD.csv fetched over HTTPS from an upstream service, plus the run date supplied as the script's first argument by cron; the warehouse loader is a Python script the shell script wraps.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single bash script starts with '#!/usr/bin/env bash' and 'set -euo pipefail'; it reads the run date from $1, builds dated file and log paths with variables and command substitution, creates a temp dir and registers 'trap cleanup EXIT', downloads with a retry-with-backoff function, validates the file is present and non-empty with if/[ tests, runs the Python loader with output redirected to a timestamped log, and returns exit 0 on success or a non-zero code on any failure that cron reads.
processingSteps: 1. Cron invokes './nightly_load.sh 2026-07-01' at 02:00. The kernel reads the shebang and runs bash on the file; 'set -euo pipefail' arms fail-fast behavior, and 'trap cleanup EXIT' ensures the temp directory (from mktemp -d) is removed however the run ends.

2. The script validates arguments ('if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then exit 2') and derives paths: run_date="$1", a dated download target, and log_file="/var/log/etl/nightly_${run_date}.log"; a log() function tees timestamped lines to that file.

3. It calls a download_with_retry function that runs 'curl -fsS' up to three times with exponential backoff, returning non-zero if every attempt fails; the main flow guards it with 'if ! download_with_retry ...; then exit 1'.
4. It checks the result exists and is non-empty ('if [ ! -s "$input_file" ]; then log ERROR; exit 1'), so an empty or missing export fails the run loudly instead of loading nothing.
5. It runs the loader - 'python3 load.py --date "$run_date" --input "$input_file" >> "$log_file" 2>&1' - and because set -e is on, any failure aborts the script and the trap still cleans up.

6. On success it logs a DONE line with the row count and 'exit 0'; on any failure it has already exited non-zero, so cron records a failed job and sends its failure email while the trap removes temp files.
endToEndExample.output: A day's events loaded into the warehouse, a timestamped log file recording the download attempts, the row count, and the final status, an empty temp directory (cleaned by the trap), and a shell exit code that is 0 on success or non-zero on failure for cron to act on.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Every run appends timestamped lines to a dated log via the log() function and output redirection; cron captures the script's exit code and emails on non-zero; the presence of the DONE line and the expected row count in the log confirm a healthy run, while missing lines or an ERROR line flag a problem.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Strict mode aborts on the first failing command; the download is retried with backoff before giving up; missing or empty inputs trigger an explicit 'exit 1'; distinct exit codes separate usage errors (2) from data/runtime errors (1); and 'trap cleanup EXIT' guarantees temp files are removed even when the script aborts.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A robust, self-documenting nightly job that runs unattended under cron, retries transient download failures, refuses to proceed on bad input, logs everything for auditing, cleans up after itself, and signals success or failure through its exit code - a textbook example of shell as reliable pipeline glue.

industryUseCases.company: Retail analytics teams running nightly warehouse loads
industryUseCases.problem: Nightly imports of sales exports were run by hand, with no consistent logging and no reliable way for the scheduler to know when a load had actually failed on a missing or empty file.
industryUseCases.solution: A parameterized bash wrapper started by cron validates the input file, runs the Python loader, logs with timestamps to a dated file, and exits non-zero on any failure so cron's alerting fires.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, auditable nightly loads, automatic failure alerts instead of silent bad runs, and a one-command, repeatable process any on-call engineer can run or re-run safely.

industryUseCases.company: Data platform teams doing large historical backfills
industryUseCases.problem: Backfilling months of daily files meant tediously re-running the same steps for each date, with mistakes when a file was missing and no clean way to resume.
industryUseCases.solution: A loop-based script iterates over a date range, checks each daily file exists, loads it, counts successes and failures, cleans up temp workspace via trap, and reports a summary while exiting non-zero if any day failed.
industryUseCases.benefits: Hundreds of days processed with a single command, per-day error isolation so one bad file does not abort the batch, and idempotent re-runs that make backfills fast and safe.

industryUseCases.company: Integration teams pulling data from flaky third-party APIs
industryUseCases.problem: External data feeds intermittently timed out or returned errors, and naive one-shot downloads failed the whole pipeline whenever the upstream had a transient hiccup.
industryUseCases.solution: A function-based script wraps the download in a retry loop with exponential backoff using 'curl -f', verifies the file before loading, and only proceeds when the fetch truly succeeds, failing the job cleanly if all retries are exhausted.
industryUseCases.benefits: Far fewer spurious pipeline failures from transient upstream issues, clear logs of each attempt for debugging, and reusable download/load functions shared across many integration scripts.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Keep each script small, single-purpose, and parameterized so the same code runs for one date or thousands; fan out invocations from a scheduler rather than baking loops into one monster script, and parallelize independent work with '&' plus 'wait' or 'xargs -P' when a backfill needs to run many days at once.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Design scripts to be idempotent and resumable: write to temp files and atomically move them into place only on success, skip work that is already done, and wrap flaky external calls (downloads, network moves) in retry-with-backoff loops so transient errors do not fail the whole job.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Do not rely on a script staying alive in an interactive session; run recurring jobs under a supervisor or scheduler (cron, systemd timers, Airflow) that restarts or reschedules on failure, and make the script's exit code the single source of truth the scheduler acts on.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Keep scripts in version control so a rebuilt host can restore them exactly, store logs off the ephemeral machine so post-mortem history survives a crash, and make jobs replayable by date/argument so any lost run can simply be re-invoked with the same parameters.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Minimize process launches inside hot loops (each external command is a fork/exec), prefer a single pass with tools like find/awk/xargs over per-item invocations, avoid re-reading large files repeatedly, and hand heavy data crunching to a purpose-built program rather than looping in bash.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Fail fast with 'set -e' so compute is not wasted on doomed runs, add idempotency checks that skip already-completed work, keep glue in lightweight shell instead of spinning up heavy runtimes for simple file moves, and schedule jobs during off-peak windows where infrastructure is cheaper.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Never hard-code secrets - read them from environment variables or a secrets manager and keep them out of logs; quote every variable to prevent word-splitting, globbing, and injection; validate and sanitize any argument used in paths or commands; avoid running as root; and be extremely cautious with 'rm' where an empty variable could expand dangerously.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Log each run with timestamps to dated files, redirect both stdout and stderr ('>> file 2>&1'), record start, key milestones, row counts, and the final status, expose success/failure through the exit code, and emit machine-parseable summary lines so schedulers and dashboards can track outcomes.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Before treating a step as done, verify the input is present and non-empty ('[ -s file ]'), check expected row counts or checksums, and refuse to publish partial or empty output; on failure, exit non-zero so the bad result never propagates downstream.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Standardize a log() helper that timestamps every line, keep one dated log per run for auditability, and drive alerting from the exit code (cron email, or a notification command on failure) plus explicit ERROR lines, so an unexpected failure or missing progress is surfaced quickly to the on-call engineer.

recommendedPractices: **Start every script with a shebang and 'set -euo pipefail':** declare '#!/usr/bin/env bash' and enable strict mode so the script fails fast on errors, unset variables, and broken pipes.
**Always quote your variables:** use "$var" (and "$@") everywhere to survive spaces, empty values, and globbing, preventing a whole class of silent bugs and dangerous 'rm' mistakes.
**Validate inputs before doing work:** check the argument count with $#, confirm files exist and are non-empty with '[ -s file ]', and exit with a clear non-zero code when a precondition fails.

**Log with timestamps and exit with meaningful codes:** use a log() helper, redirect stdout/stderr to a dated file, and 'exit 0' on success or a specific non-zero code on failure so the scheduler can react.
**Clean up with trap:** register 'trap cleanup EXIT' to remove temp files and release locks no matter how the script ends, including under set -e or Ctrl+C.
engineeringStandards: Make scripts idempotent and resumable - write to temp files and move them into place only on success, and skip work that is already complete so a re-run is always safe.
Wrap flaky external steps (downloads, network operations) in a retry loop with exponential backoff, retrying only on transient errors and giving up cleanly after a maximum.
Keep secrets out of scripts and logs - read them from environment variables or a secrets manager, and never echo them.
designRecommendations: Keep each script small and single-purpose, and parameterize it via arguments so the same code serves one date or a whole backfill instead of hard-coding values.
Factor repeated logic into functions (and shared, sourced library files) so common tasks like logging and retrying are written once and reused.
For anything recurring or critical, run the script under a scheduler or supervisor (cron, systemd, Airflow) rather than by hand, and let the exit code be the contract.
namingConventions: Use lowercase, descriptive script names with a .sh extension and a verb (run_etl.sh, fetch_and_load.sh) so intent is obvious.
Name UPPER_CASE for constants/configuration (DATA_DIR, MAX_RETRIES) and lower_case for local/loop variables (run_date, input_file) to signal scope and intent.
Name log files by job and date (etl_2026-07-01.log) so they are easy to find, rotate, and correlate with a specific run.
documentationStandards: Put a usage comment near the top of every script showing how to invoke it and what each argument means (e.g. 'Usage: ./run_etl.sh YYYY-MM-DD').
Comment the non-obvious lines - why 'set -euo pipefail', what the trap cleans up, and what each exit code means - not the obvious ones.
Document where logs are written, how to re-run safely, and any external dependencies (Python scripts, tools, credentials) the script relies on.
testingStrategies: Test the happy path and the failure paths: run with a valid input, a missing input, and an empty input, and confirm the exit code is 0 or the expected non-zero value each time.
Use 'bash -n script.sh' to catch syntax errors without running it, and run a linter like ShellCheck to flag quoting and portability bugs before shipping.
Trace tricky logic with 'set -x' (or 'bash -x script.sh') to see each expanded command, and test that the trap actually cleans up when the script is interrupted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting spaces around the = in a variable assignment, e.g. 'run_date = "$1"'.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Most programming languages allow (or require) spaces around assignment, so it feels natural, and the resulting error message ('run_date: command not found') is cryptic to beginners.
commonMistakes.impact: The assignment silently does not happen; the shell tries to run 'run_date' as a command, the variable stays unset, and later '$run_date' expands to empty, corrupting paths and logic downstream.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Write assignments with no spaces: 'run_date="$1"'. If you need spaces for readability, that is not possible for assignment - use no spaces around = and rely on quoting for the value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving variables unquoted, e.g. 'rm $file' or 'if [ $x = yes ]'.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Simple examples online often omit quotes, and scripts appear to work fine in testing where values happen to have no spaces or are never empty.
commonMistakes.impact: A value with spaces gets split into multiple arguments and an empty value can vanish, so 'rm $file' may delete the wrong files and '[ $x = yes ]' can throw a syntax error when $x is empty - subtle, sometimes destructive bugs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always quote expansions: 'rm "$file"', 'if [ "$x" = yes ]', and '"$@"' for all arguments. Prefer '[[ ... ]]' in bash, which is more forgiving, and reserve unquoted expansion only where word-splitting is intended.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the script stops on the first error, so failures are ignored and later steps run on bad data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: By default the shell keeps going after a failing command (it only prints the error), which contradicts the intuition from most languages where an unhandled error halts execution.
commonMistakes.impact: A failed download or transform does not stop the script; subsequent steps run on missing or partial data, the script may still exit 0, and the scheduler thinks the job succeeded while corrupt results flow downstream.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Enable 'set -euo pipefail' at the top so any failure aborts the script, check '$?' or use 'if ! cmd; then' where you need custom handling, and call 'exit 1' explicitly when you detect a problem so failure is unmistakable.

comparisonSection.explanation: './script.sh' asks the OS to execute the file directly, which requires execute permission ('chmod +x') and uses whatever interpreter the shebang names - the standard, self-documenting way to ship a script. 'bash script.sh' starts a fresh bash and tells it to read the file, ignoring the shebang and not needing execute permission, which is handy for a quick test or a non-executable file. Prefer a shebang plus chmod +x for anything you ship.

'[ ... ]' is the portable POSIX test command available in every shell, but it is picky: unquoted empty variables cause syntax errors and it does not support && or pattern matching. '[[ ... ]]' is a bash keyword that is safer with unquoted variables, supports && / || inside the brackets, and adds pattern and regex matching. Use '[[ ]]' in bash scripts for safety and features; use '[ ]' only when you need strict POSIX sh portability.

comparisonSection.feature: Choosing the tool for the job
comparisonSection.explanation: Shell is unbeatable for glue: launching programs, moving files, checking existence, looping over inputs, and wiring steps into a scheduler with clear exit codes, all with zero setup. Python wins the moment you need real data structures, non-trivial math, robust parsing, testing, or logic beyond a few dozen lines, where shell becomes fragile and hard to maintain. A common pattern is a thin shell wrapper that handles orchestration and calls a Python program that does the heavy lifting.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a shebang, and why do you make a script executable with chmod +x?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A shebang is the first line of a script, like '#!/bin/bash' or '#!/usr/bin/env bash', that tells the operating system which interpreter should run the file. 'chmod +x script.sh' marks the file as executable so you are allowed to run it directly as './script.sh'; without execute permission you would get 'Permission denied' and would have to run it as 'bash script.sh' instead. Together, a shebang plus chmod +x let a text file behave like a real program.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the basic mental model of how a script becomes runnable and why the first line and permissions matter. Mentioning './script.sh' versus 'bash script.sh' shows practical understanding.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you set and use a variable in bash, and what is the most common beginner mistake?
beginnerQuestions.answer: You assign with 'name=value' and there must be no spaces around the equals sign; you read it as '$name' or, better, '"$name"' in double quotes. The most common mistake is putting spaces around = (like 'name = value'), which the shell treats as running a command 'name' instead of assigning. The second most common is forgetting to quote when reading, which breaks on values that contain spaces or are empty.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress the no-spaces rule and quoting, since those are the two errors nearly every beginner hits. Naming why quoting matters (word-splitting, empty values) demonstrates hands-on experience.

intermediateQuestions.question: What does 'set -euo pipefail' do, and why is it recommended?
intermediateQuestions.answer: It combines three safety options: '-e' makes the script exit immediately if any command fails, '-u' makes referencing an unset variable an error (catching typos), and '-o pipefail' makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last one. By default the shell keeps going after failures and treats unset variables as empty strings, which hides bugs; strict mode turns those silent, dangerous behaviors into loud, immediate failures, which is essential for reliable pipeline scripts.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key insight is fail-fast versus the shell's forgiving defaults. Explaining each flag and giving the pipefail example (a failing early stage in a pipe) shows real depth.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does a script signal success or failure, and how would a scheduler like cron know a job failed?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Every command returns an exit code: 0 for success, non-zero for failure, and the last command's code is in '$?'. A script sets its own exit code with 'exit N' or by the last command it runs, and cron reads that final exit code to decide whether the job succeeded. So to make failures visible you enable 'set -e' to abort on errors and call 'exit 1' when you detect a problem; if a broken script still exits 0, cron thinks it passed and bad data flows downstream.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want you to connect exit codes to scheduler behavior. Emphasize that returning the right code is the contract between the script and its orchestrator.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you make a shell-driven ETL step robust: cleanup on failure, retries for flaky steps, and safe re-runs?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use 'trap cleanup EXIT' so temp files are removed and locks released however the script ends, including under set -e or Ctrl+C. Wrap flaky external steps (like downloads) in a retry loop with exponential backoff, retrying only on transient errors and giving up after a maximum with a non-zero return. Make the job idempotent and resumable by writing to temp files and atomically moving them into place only on success, checking whether work is already done, and validating inputs ('[ -s file ]') before proceeding - so any kill, crash, or re-run is safe and never publishes partial output.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests production maturity: trap-based cleanup, retry-with-backoff, and idempotent/atomic writes. Bonus for noting that trap runs even when set -e aborts the script.

advancedQuestions.question: What is the difference between [ ] and [[ ]], and when would you use each?
advancedQuestions.answer: '[ ]' is the POSIX 'test' command available in every shell; it is portable but strict - unquoted or empty variables can cause syntax errors, and it does not support && or pattern matching inside it. '[[ ]]' is a bash keyword that is safer with unquoted variables, supports && / || and pattern/regex matching, and generally has fewer surprises. Use '[[ ]]' in bash scripts for safety and features; use '[ ]' only when you must stay POSIX-portable (a '#!/bin/sh' script). For numeric comparisons, '(( ))' is often clearer.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The interviewer checks that you know the portability-versus-safety trade-off and the practical rule of thumb. Mentioning '(( ))' for arithmetic is a nice extra.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A nightly cron job that wraps a Python loader keeps 'succeeding' (cron sends no alerts), yet the warehouse table is sometimes empty. The script downloads a file, then runs the loader. How do you find and fix the problem?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: If cron reports success but data is missing, the script is almost certainly exiting 0 despite a real failure. First suspect: no 'set -e', so a failed download or an empty file does not stop the script, and the last command still returns 0. Second suspect: the download 'succeeds' on an error page (curl without -f) or produces an empty file that the loader happily loads as zero rows. I would check whether the script validates the input exists and is non-empty, whether it uses strict mode, and whether it propagates the loader's exit code. The fix is to fail loudly on every failure path.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Add 'set -euo pipefail' so any failing command aborts the script. Use 'curl -fsS' so HTTP errors become non-zero exits, and after downloading, validate with 'if [ ! -s "$input" ]; then echo ERROR >&2; exit 1; fi' to reject empty files. Ensure the loader's failure propagates (run it directly under set -e, or check '$?') and 'exit 1' on any detected problem so cron sees a non-zero code and alerts. Add timestamped logging and a trap for cleanup. After these changes, an empty or failed download fails the job loudly instead of silently loading nothing.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a reusable shell-based framework for the team's nightly data-loading jobs so they are consistent, observable, safe to re-run, and integrate cleanly with the scheduler.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Create a shared library (sourced with '. lib.sh') providing a timestamped log() function, a download_with_retry() with exponential backoff, and helpers for validation and atomic moves. Each job is a thin, parameterized script with '#!/usr/bin/env bash' and 'set -euo pipefail', reading the run date from an argument, building dated log paths, registering 'trap cleanup EXIT', validating inputs, running the work, and exiting 0 or a specific non-zero code. Run all jobs under cron (or Airflow), redirect output to dated logs, and let the exit code drive alerting.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Shell keeps the framework lightweight, dependency-free, and easy for any engineer to read and run, but it is fragile for complex logic and hard to unit-test thoroughly; pushing heavy transformation into Python called by the shell wrapper balances simplicity of orchestration against the robustness of a real language. A shared library reduces duplication but adds a dependency each script must source correctly.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Parameterize every job so one script serves one date or a full backfill, fan out invocations from the scheduler, and parallelize independent runs with '&'/'wait' or 'xargs -P'. Centralize logs and drive alerting from exit codes; make jobs idempotent and atomic so re-runs and node replacements never corrupt data. As complexity grows, migrate orchestration to Airflow while keeping the per-task work as small, well-tested shell or Python.

followUpQuestions: What is the difference between '>' , '>>' , and '2>&1', and when do you use each?
How does command substitution '$(...)' work, and why is it preferred over the older backtick syntax?
What do $@, $*, $#, and $0 each mean, and how do "$@" and "$*" differ when quoted?
How would you debug a misbehaving script - what do 'set -x', 'bash -n', and ShellCheck each give you?
When would you choose Python over a shell script for a pipeline task, and how do you combine the two?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A shell script is an executable text file of commands run by bash; it starts with a shebang, uses variables (name=value), reads arguments ($1, $@), checks exit codes ($?), branches and loops with if/for/while, and should use 'set -euo pipefail' and 'trap' to fail fast and clean up.
keyConcepts: The shebang (#!/usr/bin/env bash) names the interpreter; 'chmod +x' plus './script.sh' runs it, while 'bash script.sh' ignores the shebang.
Assign variables with no spaces (name=value) and always read them quoted ("$var"); use $(...) to capture command output.
Positional args are $1, $2, $@ (all), $#; every command returns an exit code in $? (0 = success, non-zero = failure).
Control flow: if/elif/else/fi with [ ] or [[ ]], for and while loops, and case; exit codes drive the branching.
'set -euo pipefail' makes scripts fail fast; 'trap cleanup EXIT' guarantees cleanup; redirect with > >> 2>&1.
commands: chmod +x run_etl.sh && ./run_etl.sh 2026-07-01   # make executable, then run
set -euo pipefail                                # strict mode: fail fast on errors/unset/pipe
run_date="$1"; echo "date=$run_date args=$#"     # read an argument, no spaces around =
if [ ! -f "$input" ]; then echo missing >&2; exit 1; fi   # check file, exit non-zero on failure
for f in /data/raw/events_*.csv; do echo "$f"; done       # loop over dated input files
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT                        # always clean up temp files on exit
interviewPoints: Shebang + chmod +x make a file runnable as ./script.sh; bash script.sh ignores the shebang.
No spaces around = in assignments; always quote "$var" to avoid word-splitting and empties.
Exit code (0 vs non-zero, in $?) is the contract with schedulers - exit 1 on failure.
'set -euo pipefail' turns silent failures into immediate stops; the shell does NOT stop on errors by default.
Use trap for cleanup, retry-with-backoff for flaky steps, and idempotent writes for safe re-runs.
quickNotes: 'name = value' is a bug - it runs a command 'name'; assignment needs no spaces.
'$?' holds the last command's exit code; 'if cmd; then' branches on that code.
'2>&1' merges stderr into stdout; put it AFTER the '> file' redirect.
'$(date +%F)' gives today's date for dated logs and filenames.
'./script.sh' needs execute permission; 'bash script.sh' does not but ignores the shebang.

keyTakeaways: A shell script is just a file of commands run top to bottom by an interpreter; the shebang (#!/usr/bin/env bash) names that interpreter, and 'chmod +x' plus './script.sh' turns the file into a runnable program (while 'bash script.sh' bypasses the shebang).

Master the fundamentals precisely: assign variables with no spaces (name=value), always read them quoted ("$var"), capture output with command substitution $(...), read inputs from $1/$@/$#, and treat the exit code in $? (0 = success, non-zero = failure) as the signal a scheduler acts on.
Control flow - if/elif/else with [ ] or [[ ]], for and while loops, and case - lets a script validate inputs, loop over dated files, and make decisions, all built on the exit codes commands return.

Reliable scripts fail fast and clean up: put 'set -euo pipefail' at the top so errors, unset variables, and broken pipes stop the run immediately, use 'trap cleanup EXIT' to remove temp files no matter how it ends, and 'exit 1' explicitly on detected failures so the scheduler sees them.

Shell is ideal glue for real DE workflows - wrapping Python jobs, checking files exist, retrying flaky downloads with backoff, logging with timestamps, and returning a clear exit code so cron or Airflow detects failure - but reach for Python once logic grows complex, and let the exit code be the contract between script and orchestrator.
